General Characterization

	The sources listed above indicate ways in which KoinÃ© (or
Hellenistic) Greek differs from Classical Greek. The following is a
summary of some of the main points they raise. 

	Robertson characterizes KoinÃ© Greek as a later development
of Classical Greek, that is, the dialect spoken in Attica (the region
around Athens) during the classical period. 

To all intents and purposes the vernacular ÎºÎ¿Î¹Î½Î® is the later
vernacular Attic with normal development under historical environment
created by Alexander's conquests.  On this base then were deposited varied
influences from the other dialects, but not enough to change the essential
Attic character of the language (Robertson, 71). 

If the KoinÃ© is an outgrowth of Classical Greek, what are the
differences between the two?  Robertson states the basic differences
succinctly.  KoinÃ© was more practical than academic, putting the
stress on clarity rather than eloquence.  Its grammar was simplified,
exceptions were decreased and generalized, inflections were dropped or
harmonized, and sentence-construction made easier.  KoinÃ©  was the
language of life and not of books.

Accidence

There is quite a bit of difference with reference to accidence.  The Ionic
substantive form -ÏÎ·Ï takes precedence over
the Attic form -ÏÎ±Ï.
Possessive adjectives, which Classical Greek used for
the emphatic possessive genitive of the personal pronoun, have to a great
extent disappeared in KoinÃ©  and have been replaced by the personal
pronoun in the genitive.  The system used to express degrees of comparison
in adjectives has been simplified, since superlative forms have mostly
disappeared (comparative forms being used in their place) and what
vestigial superlatives remain are used mostly in the elative sense. 

It is with respect to the verb that most change in accidence has occurred.
First, there are no dual forms in KoinÃ©.  Secondly, the future tense
has retreated.  That is, alternative forms are eliminated in that tense; 
the (non-periphrastic) future perfect is mostly eliminated; the simple
perfect is limited mostly to the indicative mood;  and the future
participle is becoming disused.  However, the future indicative is taking
on some of the functions of the aorist subjunctive.  Thirdly, the optative
has a very limited use (which will be discussed later).  
Fourthly, verbal adjectives in -ÏÎ­Î¿Ï are lacking 
(the only NT example is in Luke 5:38), 
and those in -ÏÏÏ have been crystallized into a set group.  
Fifthly, periphrastic construction is on the increase.  
Sixthly, the pluperfect in KoinÃ© no longer requires the augment, 
and the tense sign becomes -ÎºÎµÎ¹- instead of -ÎºÎµ-.
Lastly, the passive is beginning to gain the ascendancy over the middle
voice. Most of these trends can be seen to have carried on into Modern
Greek.

Syntax

There are many differences between Classical Greek and KoinÃ© in
syntax.  KoinÃ© has shorter sentences, more parataxis and less
hypotaxis, a sparing use of participles, and a growth in the use of
prepositions (although some old ones have died out).  Variations of nouns,
adjectives, and verbs are often according to sense, and a neuter plural
substantive may be used with either a singular or a plural verb. 
KoinÃ© used personal pronouns in oblique cases much more often,
whereas writers in Attic used them only when they were necessary for
clarity.  

One of the biggest syntactical differences involves the use of the
optative mood.  Blass notes three Classical uses of this mood.  The first
is to denote an attainable wish.  This use still occurs in the Septuagint,
the New Testament, and the papyri, but there is a strong tendency to use
the imperative in requests and imprecations.  Attic Îµá¼´Î¸Îµ and Îµá¼° Î³Î¬Ï do
not occur with the optative in KoinÃ© (nor do they occur with the
indicative to show an unattainable wish);  rather á½ÏÎµÎ»Î¿Î½
with the future indicative is employed.  
The second use is the potential optative in a main clause with á¼Î½ 
to denote what is thought. 
This use has mostly disappeared, although it does occur in some apodoses of conditional
sentences.  
The future indicative or the subjunctive often replaces the
potential optative.  The third use of the optative is that in indirect
discourse.  KoinÃ© uses this function very little; in fact, it uses
indirect discourse very little.  The iterative optative in subordinate
clauses is supplanted by á¼Î½ and the imperfect
or aorist indicative.  Dana says the optative in indirect discourse occurs
only three times in the NT but he makes no mention at all of the optative
with a secondary tense of verbs of fearing.   

In Classical Greek there were five types of conditional sentences (using
Blass's classification):  1) real conditions (Îµá¼° with the indicative), 
2) contrary-to-fact conditions (Îµá¼°  with an augmented tense of the indicative), 
3) conditions of more vivid expectation (á¼Î¬Î½ with the subjunctive), 
4) conditions of less vivid expectation (á¼Î¬Î½ with the potential optative), 
and 5) repetition in past time (Îµá¼° with the optative).  In KoinÃ©, type 1
(real conditions) has lost ground, type 2 (contrary-to-fact conditions) 
persists, type 3 (more vivid conditions)  prevails, type 4 (less vivid
conditions) is barely represented, and type 5 (repetition in past time) 
has disappeared. One Classical feature that KoinÃ© does not have is the
conditional relative clause, in which the indefinite pronoun substitutes
for the conditional conjunction.  

Another syntactical feature of Classical Greek missing in KoinÃ© is
the object clause.  After a verb of striving, caring, or effecting,
Classical Greek uses á½ÏÏÏ with the future indicative for the object, 
but KoinÃ© does not.
